title: The Parthian Empire
description: An illustrated map of the Parthian Empire, from Arsaces and the horsemen of Nisa through Mithridates I’s conquests, Ctesiphon and the envoys of Han China, to the Roman disaster at Carrhae, the struggle for Armenia, Trajan at the Gulf, Hatra’s walls and the rise of Ardashir.
mapLabel: Illustrated map of the Parthian Empire, from about 247 BCE to today
note: Few Parthian records survive, so the story leans on Greek, Roman and Chinese writers (Polybius, Strabo, Plutarch, Tacitus, Cassius Dio and Sima Qian), on coins, Babylonian tablets and excavated sites; each chapter says which it follows. Roman writers were not neutral, and their numbers for armies and the dead are uncertain. Kings’ dates are often approximate. Places in Bactria and China lie beyond the map’s eastern edge, so routes run off the map towards them. Native names are given in Latin letters. The map is stylised and not to scale. Lands under Powers are painted loosely.

steps.title: Arsaces and the Parni
steps.text: The Parni, horse-riding people from the steppe east of the Caspian, led by Arsaces, take the Seleucid province of Parthia, traditionally in about 238 BCE. Parthian dating later counts its years from 247 BCE, perhaps when Arsaces became chief. Every later king puts the name Arsaces on his coins, so the dynasty is called the Arsacids.
steps.today: Today: Old Nisa, near Ashgabat, Turkmenistan; a World Heritage Site.

steps.title: The city of a hundred gates
steps.text: The Seleucid king Antiochus III marches east to win back his lost lands and takes Hecatompylos, the Parthian royal city whose Greek name means “a hundred gates”. Polybius tells how the Parthians tried to block the wells on his way. Arsaces II makes peace and accepts him as overlord, but once Antiochus leaves, Parthia goes its own way.
steps.today: Today: Shahr-e Qumis, a field of ruined mounds near Damghan, Iran.

steps.title: Mithridates I takes Media
steps.text: Mithridates I turns a frontier kingdom into an empire. In about 148 BCE he takes Media, with its old royal city Ecbatana, which becomes a summer capital of Parthian kings. His coins call him philhellene, “friend of the Greeks”, to win over the Greek cities he now rules. Persis and Elymais in the south-west also come under Parthian overlordship.
steps.today: Today: Hamadan, Iran. The mound of Hegmataneh, in the city centre, is being excavated.

steps.title: Into Mesopotamia
steps.text: Babylonian tablets record Mithridates I in Seleucia on the Tigris in 141 BCE: Babylonia is Parthian. Across the river, Ctesiphon grows from an army camp into the kings’ winter residence and, in time, the capital. In 129 BCE his son Phraates II defeats and kills the Seleucid Antiochus VII, who had marched to take the east back.
steps.today: Today: Salman Pak, south-east of Baghdad, Iraq. Seleucia’s ruins lie just across the Tigris.

steps.title: Envoys from Han China
steps.text: Mithridates II wins back the east from nomad invaders and holds Merv. Envoys of the Han emperor Wu arrive; the historian Sima Qian calls the country Anxi. He records silver coins with the king’s face, writing set sideways on leather, and Parthian gifts sent to China: ostrich eggs and conjurors. The Silk Road now runs through Parthia.
steps.today: Today: Merv, beside Mary, Turkmenistan; a World Heritage Site.

steps.title: King of kings
steps.text: Mithridates II takes the old Persian title king of kings, and at Behistun a relief shows four nobles before him, near Darius’s great inscription. In 96 BCE his envoy meets the Roman Sulla on the Euphrates, the first meeting of the two powers; Plutarch says the king later executed his envoy for letting Sulla take the seat of honour.
steps.today: Today: Bisotun, Kermanshah province, Iran. A seventeenth-century inscription was cut across the Parthian relief.

steps.title: Disaster at Carrhae
steps.text: The Roman general Crassus invades with seven legions. Near Carrhae, the Parthian commander Surena, with about 10,000 horsemen, mostly mounted archers kept supplied with arrows by a camel train, destroys his army. Plutarch says 20,000 Romans died and 10,000 were captured; the figures are uncertain. Crassus is killed at a parley, and the legions’ eagle standards are taken.
steps.today: Today: Harran, Şanlıurfa province, Turkey, known for its beehive-shaped mud-brick houses.

steps.title: Antony’s retreat, Augustus’s deal
steps.text: Mark Antony invades through Armenia in 36 BCE with, Plutarch says, about 100,000 men, besieges Phraaspa in Media and retreats with heavy losses. Augustus chooses a deal instead of war: in 20 BCE Phraates IV hands back the eagles taken at Carrhae, which Rome celebrates as a victory. Armenia becomes the prize both empires fight over.
steps.today: Today: the ruins of Artaxata, near the monastery of Khor Virap, Armenia, below Mount Ararat.

steps.title: A Parthian prince crowned by Nero
steps.text: Vologases I puts his brother Tiridates on Armenia’s throne, and war with Rome follows. After a Roman army surrenders at Rhandeia in 62 CE, the two sides agree: a Parthian prince will rule Armenia, but be crowned by Rome. In 66 CE Tiridates travels to Rome and Nero crowns him. His family rules Armenia for centuries.
steps.today: Today: Artashat, Armenia, a town near the old city, takes its name.

steps.title: Trajan reaches the Gulf
steps.text: In 116 CE the emperor Trajan takes Ctesiphon and sails down to the Persian Gulf; Cassius Dio says he watched a ship leave for India and wished he were young enough to follow Alexander. Revolts break out, and his successor Hadrian gives the conquests back. Roman armies sack Ctesiphon again in 165 and 198 CE.
steps.today: Today: Salman Pak, Iraq. The great arch standing there, the Taq Kasra, is later and Sasanian.

steps.title: Hatra holds out
steps.text: Hatra, a walled desert city whose rulers called themselves kings of the Arabs under Parthian overlords, grows rich on caravans and its great temple of the sun god Shamash. Its walls turn back Trajan in 117 CE and Septimius Severus twice, in 198 and 199 CE. Its temples, statues and inscriptions in Aramaic survived until modern times.
steps.today: Today: al-Hadr, Iraq; a World Heritage Site, damaged by the Islamic State group in 2015.

steps.title: Ardashir ends the Arsacids
steps.text: In Persis (Fars), a local ruler, Ardashir, rebels. In 224 CE, at Hormozdgan, a battlefield whose site is disputed, he defeats and kills Artabanus IV, the last great Parthian king. By 226 he holds Ctesiphon and is crowned king of kings: the Sasanian dynasty begins. Parthian noble houses such as the Suren and Karen serve the new kings.
steps.today: Today: Salman Pak, Iraq. Ardashir’s own story is told in The Sasanian Empire.

steps.title: Nisa dug up
steps.text: Soviet archaeologists began large digs at Old Nisa in 1946; an Italian team has worked there since 1990. Over 2,700 inscribed potsherds (ostraca), mostly records of wine deliveries, preserve the Parthian language and give the fortress its old name, Mihrdatkirt, “fortress of Mithridates”. Carved ivory drinking horns (rhyta) show how Greek and Iranian art mixed.
steps.today: Today: Old Nisa, Turkmenistan. The ivory horns are in museums in Ashgabat and St Petersburg.

items.name: Arsaces I
items.text: Arsaces led the Parni into Parthia. Almost nothing certain is known of his life; Greek and Roman writers give different stories of his origins, and his dates are disputed. His coins show a seated archer holding a bow, a design kept by Parthian kings for centuries, and every king after him took his name as a throne name.

items.name: Mithridates I
items.text: Mithridates I took Media, Persis and Babylonia from the Seleucids and made Parthia an empire from the Euphrates to the borders of Bactria. He ruled over Greek cities and Babylonian temples alike, and called himself friend of the Greeks on his coins. Historians count him the empire’s true founder.

items.name: Mithridates II
items.text: Mithridates II drove back the nomads who had killed two kings before him and pushed Parthian power into Armenia. He was the first Arsacid to call himself king of kings, a title of the old Persian kings, and in his reign Parthia made contact with both Rome and Han China.

items.name: Surena
items.text: Surena was the head of the Suren family, which had the right to crown Parthian kings; his personal name is not recorded. Plutarch calls him tall and handsome, wearing face paint and travelling with a thousand baggage camels. Not long after Carrhae, King Orodes II had him put to death, Plutarch says out of envy.

items.name: Musa
items.text: Musa was an Italian slave woman whom Augustus sent as a gift to Phraates IV. She became his queen, and their son became Phraates V. Josephus says she had a hand in Phraates IV’s death. Her portrait appears on coins beside her son’s, a rare honour for a Parthian queen. Nobles soon drove both out.

items.name: Tiridates I
items.life: king of Armenia from about 52 CE
items.text: A brother of Vologases I and a Zoroastrian priest (magus), Tiridates travelled to Rome by land, Pliny says, because as a magus he would not defile the sea. Nero crowned him in the Forum in 66 CE. He began the Arsacid line of Armenian kings, which lasted until 428 CE.
